chunks.title: THE CLAIMANT
chunks.transcript:
Forty years of apparent foreknowledge and I had required years to establish that events had changed.

“I was busy.”

Ithar did not move.

“Being nineteen again.”

Still nothing.

I had seen that silence before.

Usually after saying something about people that he understood as words and not as a fact.

“You don't get that part.”

His eye dropped to my leg.

I looked down too.

“Explaining knees to a dragon that still has all of his is going to annoy me.”

chunks.title: THE CLAIMANT
chunks.transcript:
Maybe twelve depending when you counted the first contract people started calling S-class work before the Authority changed the badge.

I could cross an active pressure break without a shield crew.

I could hold full reinforcement most of a day if I wasn't doing anything stupid.

Usually I was doing something stupid.

“I killed a redback alone north of Vey.”

That got him.

Not much.

An inch of head movement from Ithar was becoming the equivalent of another creature standing up.

chunks.title: THE CLAIMANT
chunks.transcript:
“But errors are shaped by where a mind stood when it made them. You remember the membrane from above it. You remember believing it was armor because you were trying to put a sword through an animal that wanted you dead. You remember the smell before you remember the mechanism. Your misunderstanding is consistent with having survived an event rather than studied one.

“That does not prove your explanation. It makes the error useful.”

I shifted against the wall.

chunks.title: THE CLAIMANT
chunks.transcript:
“A secret is not made supernatural by being secret. Names move. Instructions move. Maps move. A person tells another person. A page is copied. A threat is overheard. A debtor repays a favor. A dying creature says something it had intended to keep. Every piece of knowledge has a history even when the history is hidden.

“You recognize this disk. There is a path by which you might have learned it, even if neither of us can yet identify that path.

chunks.title: THE BARGAINER
chunks.transcript:
That worried me.

A person should not become accustomed to sitting beside enough money to destabilize a kingdom.

Then again, people become accustomed to most things if they happen around breakfast often enough.

I had learned that twice.

The dragon let me finish trying to negotiate before he answered.

chunks.title: THE BARGAINER
chunks.transcript:
Recover the horse, if the horse had developed a conscience.

Then what?

The question did not need his voice every time.

I could hear it anyway.

Then what?

Then what?

Then what?

“You could do this forever.”

The dragon did not disagree.

“And then I live.”

Ithar went still.

Not interested still.

Different.

The kind that meant I had stepped on something without hearing it crack yet.

He did not need a long answer for that one.

“You have already done that twice.”

chunks.title: THE BARGAINER
chunks.transcript:
The dragon had watched me move before the stone in a way my leg could not presently support.

Luck, I could have called it.

Training.

Just not this body's training.

I scratched at my jaw.

The beard had gotten rough during the climb.

There had been a time when three days without shaving felt like neglect.

Then I had children.

Then I had worse problems.

Then I had fewer reasons to care.

The memory arrived and left before I could stop it.

Ithar's eye shifted.

He had not read the thought.

chunks.title: THE BARGAINER
chunks.transcript: “If you say you worked somewhere for six years, and six years are truly indistinguishable to you, I gain nothing by forcing you to invent distinctions. If you remember the first morning, a particular lunch, the person who sat across from you, the first time you were late, the day your wages changed, an argument in the third year, and the meal after your final shift, then you do not remember six years as one sentence.

chunks.title: THE BARGAINER
chunks.transcript:
“You have spent decades deciding which memories explain who you became. I have no reason to trust that selection. You know what mattered to you when you last interpreted it. That is not necessarily what mattered. The reason you remember a thing may not be the reason you believe you remember it.”

I sat with that.

I did not enjoy it.

The cave water moved somewhere behind him.

Slow and steady.

The Line moved under the continent too.

Not slow enough anymore.

“Fine.”
